identification.title: Give Thanks
identification.notes: Written by Henry Smith in 1978 in Williamsburg, Virginia, while unemployed and losing his sight, after a sermon on Christ's poverty making us rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). It reached Integrity's Hosanna! Music by way of a congregation in Germany and was published in 1986 credited to an unknown author until Smith was found. CCLI 20285. Don Moen's 1986 live recording is the one most churches know; the Maranatha! Music Praise 10 version followed in 1988. Of some 300 songs Smith wrote, it is his only published one.

claims.structuralNotes: Two short sections and nothing else. The first, sung as the verse, is an imperative to give thanks followed by the reason: God has given his Son. The second, sung as the chorus, has the weak and the poor declare themselves strong and rich because of what the Lord has done, and closes on the title phrase. About eight distinct lines; most arrangements sing the whole through two or three times.

claims.claim: Thanksgiving is owed to God, who is the Holy One.
claims.subject: Worship and the holiness of God

claims.claim: God has given Jesus Christ, his Son.
claims.subject: The gift of the Son

claims.claim: The weak may call themselves strong, and the poor rich, because of what the Lord has done for us.
claims.subject: Strength in weakness

claims.claim: The ground of thanks is God's act, not the singer's circumstances.
claims.subject: Grace

strengths.title: Thanks grounded in the gift of Christ
strengths.explanation: The reason given for gratitude is that God has given his Son. That is the New Testament's own ground for thanksgiving, and the song reaches it in its second line rather than leaving thanks free-floating.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift — the gift is Christ, and the song gives the same reason.

strengths.title: The weak are strong because of God, not effort
strengths.explanation: The chorus has the weak and the poor declare strength and riches, and the reason is what the Lord has done for us. Confidence rests on God's act rather than on the singer's resolve, which is the right place for it.
strengths.scriptureRationale: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.

strengths.title: God named as the Holy One before he is thanked
strengths.explanation: The song does not thank an unnamed you. God is named by a scriptural title in the first line and Jesus Christ by name in the second, so a visitor knows who is being thanked and for what.
strengths.scriptureRationale: I am the LORD, your Holy One — the title the song opens with.

concerns.title: Joel's battle summons borrowed for the believer
concerns.explanation: The chorus takes its wording from Joel 3:10, where the weak are told to call themselves warriors as the nations are summoned to judgment. The truth the song means — strength in weakness through God's work — is Paul's, not Joel's, and the borrowed line carries a context that does not fit.
concerns.scriptureRationale: The line is addressed to the nations gathering for battle, not to God's people in weakness — the passage the song quotes is not the one it means.

doctrinesAffirmed: Strength in weakness through God's work
Thanksgiving as the response to grace
theological.assessment: Eight lines, none of them wrong. Thanks is owed to the Holy One because he has given his Son, and the weak and poor may call themselves strong and rich because of what the Lord has done. Confidence is placed where Paul puts it. The one reservation is a borrowed text: the chorus is worded from Joel's summons to the nations, which is not about believers in weakness, so a Pauline truth is said in a prophet's unrelated words. What it lacks is scope — the cross, sin and the resurrection are never reached.

strengths.title: Owned on first hearing
strengths.explanation: A stepwise melody over a handful of lines. A room learns it inside one repetition and can carry it without a band, which almost no song written since can claim.

strengths.title: The congregation exhorts itself
strengths.explanation: The opening is an imperative addressed to the room rather than a report of anyone's feelings, and the reason clause is sung as us. It is built to be said together.

strengths.title: Fits anywhere in a service
strengths.explanation: Short enough to open a gathering, respond to a reading or close communion, and it has done all three for forty years across traditions that agree on little else.

concerns.title: Too short to stand alone
concerns.explanation: The whole song is under a minute sung once. Arrangements fill a slot by repeating it two or three times, and past the second pass nothing further is being said.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Published in F and E flat, moving mostly by step in descending phrases; comfortable for an ordinary room in either key.

range.key: Published in F; also E flat
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The title phrase returns several times by design and the whole is usually sung through twice. That is a refrain doing its job, not padding — though a third pass adds nothing.
communal.assessment: Among the easiest congregational songs in current use: a stepwise tune, eight lines, an imperative the room addresses to itself, and no dependence on an arrangement. Its only limit is its length. Sung once it is under a minute, so it is usually repeated or paired with another song, and leaders should treat it as a response or a frame rather than a set piece.

strengths.title: Every word a child can sing
strengths.explanation: Thanks, holy, given, Son, weak, strong, poor, rich. There is no image to unpack and no term to define; a newcomer knows exactly what has been affirmed.

strengths.title: Command, then reason
strengths.explanation: The verse gives the instruction and immediately the ground for it, and the chorus does the same in the other order. A hearer is never left wondering why thanks is being asked.

concerns.title: Strong and rich can be heard as money
concerns.explanation: The chorus has the poor call themselves rich because of what the Lord has done. The writer meant the exchange of 2 Corinthians 8:9, riches in Christ, but the line does not say so, and in some rooms it will be heard as a promise about money.
concerns.scriptureRationale: Christ became poor so that by his poverty we might become rich — the sense the writer intended, which the words leave open.

clarity.assessment: Plain to the point of transparency. Every line is a common word and every claim comes with its reason attached, so nothing needs explaining before a congregation can sing it and mean it. The single soft spot is the chorus's strong and rich, which the writer grounded in Christ's poverty for our sake but which the song leaves open to a material hearing in a room inclined to one.

synthesis.summary: Eight plain lines grounding thanksgiving in God's gift of his Son and placing the confidence of the weak on what the Lord has done. Nothing in it is wrong and any room can sing it unaccompanied. Its chorus is worded from Joel's summons to the nations, a borrowed text that does not fit the Pauline truth it carries, and its strong and rich can be heard as money. Best as a response or a frame; too short to carry a set.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Thanksgiving for God's inexpressible gift, which is the ground the verse gives.
Christ's poverty making us rich — the exchange behind the chorus, and the sermon that prompted the song.
Strength in weakness through grace, the truth the chorus states.
The passage the chorus is worded from — a summons to the nations rather than a promise to the weak.
